utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber has granted a request to make further submissions in relation to the production of documents obtained by the Defence. The Chamber also was copied on an e-mail exchange, in which you, Mr. Misetic, invite the Prosecution to find a factual basis for their position, and you apparently were not very satisfied with the response which said something of the kind as litigation will be in court. Is there any practical way to resolve it because, of course, the Chamber would not be amused, Mr. Waespi, if, for a lack of knowledge of the Defence, we would lose further time because they couldn't prepare for a response. But I'll talk to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes when reading some of the e-mail exchanges, I wished that, apart from having studied law, to have studied psychology as well. Then having dealt with that matter, we still owe the Prosecution a decision on a request for Prosecution motion to hear Witness 82's evidence via video-conference link, and I'll deliver the decision. I think we have given the decision, but the reasons are now delivered. On the 3rd of February, 2009, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that Witness 82's evidence be presented via video-conference link on the 16th of February. The Prosecution argued that the witness's medical condition prevents him from travelling to The Hague within the time left for the presentation of the Prosecution's case. The motion was supplemented by a medical report on the witness's health situation and a declaration from a Prosecution investigator, describing the investigator's recent telephone conversation with the witness. On the 4th of February, the Gotovina Defence submitted that the witness's condition was not such as to render him unable to travel to The Hague. The other Defence teams joined this submission. These submissions can be found at transcript pages 15712 and 15713. On the 5th of February, the Chamber informally communicated to the parties that it decided to deny the motion, without prejudice. According to Rule 81 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a chamber may order that proceedings be conducted by way of video-conference link if this is consistent with the interests of justice. As previously set out by this Chamber, the standard of Rule 81 bis is met if a witness is unable to come to The Hague if the testimony is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the requesting party to proceed without it and if the accused is not prejudiced in his or her right to confront the witness. The Chamber found that the information contained in the medical report of the 7th of January, 2009, does not depict the witness's health situation as sufficiently serious as to prevent him from travelling to The Hague. The one medical report that the Chamber received suggests that the witness's condition is not of a long duration, and moreover, the symptoms described in the report, the prescribed treatment, and the indication that the witness has responded well to therapy support this finding. In addition, the declaration of the Prosecution investigator who spoke to the witness on the telephone on the 2nd of February, 2009, in which the witness is described as having a high fever and coughing heavily is insufficient to establish that the witness is unable to travel to The Hague. Since that declaration is not a medical report, it is not -- the information in it is not verified. It lacks specificity, and it does not clarify the cause of the witness's ailments. It's not clear to the Chamber whether the symptoms explained in the investigator's declaration are in any way related to those in the medical report. The Chamber was therefore not persuaded that the witness was unable to come to the Tribunal and found that the standard of Rule 81 bis was not met. Having reached this conclusion, the Chamber did not consider the remaining two elements. For these reasons, the Chamber decided to deny the motion without prejudice, and this concludes the Chamber's reasons on the matter. Another decision to be delivered by the Chamber is a decision on the admission of an expert report and associated exhibits of Witness Harry Konings. This is a decision on the admission of the expert report of Harry Konings, marked for identification as P1259; his addendum to that report, marked for identification as P1260; the Prosecution's terms of reference for the addendum, marked for identification as P1261; and a corrigendum to the expert report and addendum, marked for identification as P1262. On the 18th of December, 2008, the Chamber filed a decision on the expert report and addendum, in which it dealt with the Defence`s objections to admission into evidence, found that it was in the interests of justice to consider the addendum for admission and deferred a final decision on the admission of the expert report and addendum until the testimony of Harry Konings. The witness testified between the 13th and the 20th of January, 2009, and on the last day, after the completion of the testimony, the Chamber invited the parties to make submissions on admission of the expert report and associated exhibits while focussing on the witness's qualification as an expert. This invitation and the parties' submissions can be found at transcript pages 14819 through 14832. The expert status of the witness as such was not disputed, although the parties disagreed on the precise scope of his expertise. The Chamber finds that the Prosecution has established during the testimony of Harry Konings his expertise in the use of artillery in military operations. It finds further that the expert report and addendum fall within this area of expertise. Having read the reports, and considered the testimony of Harry Konings, the Chamber is also satisfied that the reports meet the requirements for admission, set out in Rule 89 (C). The Gotovina Defence opposed admission into evidence, arguing that Konings had testified that at the time the Prosecution asked him to prepare the expert report, the Prosecution also announced to him that it would later request an addendum. The Prosecution stated that at that time, it had no intention to later seek an addendum and had not, to its recollection, announced any addendum. The Gotovina Defence argued that it had suffered prejudice from the late filing of the addendum by being deprived of the opportunity to put it to witnesses who had testified prior to that time. The latter argument is similar to one which the Chamber already dealt with in its decision of the 18th of December, 2008. The Chamber will address the new fact in the testimony of Konings at transcript pages 14493 through 14494, in which he indicated that the Prosecution had announced to him in advance that it would request an addendum. The Chamber may reconsider its previous decision if justified by particular circumstances in order to avoid an injustice. A new fact may constitute such a particular circumstance. Even assuming that the witness's recollection on the matter is accurate, the Chamber finds that a new fact revealed in his testimony does not create a significant change in the factual situation that was before the Chamber when it issued its decision on the 18th of December, 2008. The Defence's argument that the Prosecution had intended all along to file an addendum is pertinent for the question of whether there's good cause for late filing rather than for what burden it places on the Defence. In its previous decision, the Chamber already found that the Prosecution had not shown good cause for its late filing of the addendum. The Chamber, weighing, also, other factors, nonetheless decided to consider it for admission. Consequently, the Chamber finds that there are no particular circumstances warranting a re-consideration of its previous decision. Pursuant to these findings and those made in its decision of the 18th of December, 2008, the Chamber therefore admits into evidence P1259, P1260, P1261, and P1262. The Chamber will, in due course and in consideration of all the evidence before it, determine what weight, if any, to attribute to the evidence of Konings, including his opinions and conclusions drawn on the basis of documents and other information submitted to him by the parties. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of the expert report and associated exhibits of Witness Konings. The next item, Mr. Waespi, is submissions and a decision on protective measures for Official Notes. No real application for protective measures have been made, but the Chamber is aware of the existence of an e-mail by Ms. Mahindaratne in which she announces that the Prosecution would like to have protective measures for one of the Official Notes where a -- someone who appeared once on the witness list of the OTP is mentioned. I couldn't say at this moment that it is a very elaborate reasoning, and the Chamber wonders, also having reviewed this Official Note, what exactly is said about this person, whether the Prosecution still wants to pursue this matter.

For the next item, out of an abundance of caution, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've put this significance and importance issue in my statement at this moment to make very clear, first of all, that we've seen it; whether we wish to see it is another matter, but we have seen it, and also what our position is in relation to that is, that they are not discussing at this moment significance or importance of changes but just to get the right versions. Matters which are more on than just practicalities, and practicalities, I understand, things like, Is Mr. A available on that day or not, but really the practical things, matters that are not just of a practical nature and a bit more will be mentioned so that they appear on the record of these proceedings and matters of real significance and importance are to be filed, even if they were exchanged initially by e-mail. That's the system the Chamber has adopted and which I repeat. Now let me just ... is there -- uploading has taken place already and is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not taken place. We're ready, Your Honour, but we're waiting for this final confirmation, and the way it was going to be done was by of a filing so that it was done through the official system, and then the -- rather like we've done with agreed stipulations in the past. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, you asked for a couple of minutes to make submissions in relation to the document refilm from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record my request was to address very briefly the Prosecution's reply on the 28th of January concerning both the report and the document refilm. It's my intention, also, at the end, with Your Honours' leave, to show Your Honours a very short clip portion to demonstrate what we say is the unreliability concerning the latter, the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against -- apart from, of course, not from making submissions because that request is granted but also to play part of a very short clip portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. As Your Honour has received three filings in this matter, it is clear, I'm sure, to Your Honours by now that it's the Defence position that the heart of the submission that we make in respect of both the report and the film concerns its unreliability, which we say goes directly to the admissibility point and not the weight as has been submitted by the Prosecution. Support for this principle can be found in paragraph 9 of the Milutinovic decision of the 1st of September, 2006, which refers there to the fact that although certain earlier decisions of the Tribunal held that reliability is not a precondition for the admission of evidence, the text of the rules and more recent appellate jurisprudence makes it clear that reliability is relevant to the admissibility of the evidence, particularly where that evidence concerns an out-of-court written statement. Your Honour, we also rely upon not only that decision but the second Milutinovic decision of the 13th of September, 2006, which we've cited in the motion, and we submit that those decisions are on all fours with the challenge that faces this Trial Chamber in determining the unreliability/admissibility aspect of the matters before you. In paragraph 6, to address reply specifically, the Milutinovic approach to admissibility has been described by the Prosecution as the exception rather than the rule. I would stress, however, Your Honour, that it has come to my attention within the last few days that the decision is not one which is only relied upon by the Cermak Defence before this institution; it's also one which stretches to be pleaded before the special Court of Sierra Leone in the Charles Taylor case where a motion is pending before that Court submitted on the 5th January, 2009, relying on the Milutinovic approach concerning the admissibility of similar NGO reports. To deal briefly with several of the points that have been raised, I would draw Your Honours' attention to paragraph 3 of the Prosecution's reply where, in my submission, a narrow selection of factors to be taken into account when dealing with admissibility has been put forward. Six of the key factors, again, rooted in Milutinovic, are not set out, and Your Honour has these in the Defence motion that has been filed before the Court. I don't intend to repeat them here, as they are clearly set out. Paragraph 7 of the Prosecution's reply refers to the fact that this Trial Chamber has admitted documents previously, concerning first- and second-hand hearsay, and the reference there is to the admission of documents tendered through the UNCIVPOL witness, Mr. Jan Elleby. Your Honour, in my submission, the difference here is that it's not just a matter of first- or second-hand hearsay, but you are confronted by ten pages as set out in the Defence motion of live indicators of unreliability. Not only are the interviewers not named, but in many instances, the interviewees are listed by initial only, and in many cases, as I have sought to demonstrate through the filing of the motion, there are no footnotes at all. The Prosecution seeks to plead before you in paragraph 8 of the reply that in fact the report itself is reliable. In seeking to make that submission, they rely on the fact that the HHO, the Helsinki Committee, describes itself as having a reputation of protection and promotion of human rights and recording human rights abuses in Croatia. In my submission, that does not, however, answer the question for this Trial Chamber, which is whether or not this individual report is sufficiently reliable for the purposes of criminal proceedings given the way in which it can be seen it has been prepared and the methodology employed. The point of this report is clearly to highlight human rights abuses. The aim of the report was not, I would submit, to create an objective and factual account of what actually occurred, neither can it be replied upon for that purpose. The Prosecution seeks to persuade you further that, in fact, not one element of the report has been successfully publicly disputed. Again, in my submission, Your Honour, it does not, however, answer the question of whether in fact the methods used to prepare this report have ever previously been scrutinized before any criminal court in this context. You are referred to the fact that the report contains detailed footnotes. It does not, however, address the concerns that I have mentioned concerning a plethora of examples when no such substantive referencing is provided. You are given, what is said, corroborative evidence, but if on further inspection it would be my submission that that corroborative evidence is in many instances generic and partial. In confidential Appendix B of the reply, the Prosecution seeks to corroborate events which are not even dated in the Storm report. Paragraph 9, the Prosecution seeks to submit that the indicia of reliability which have been cited by the Defence are either erroneous or go to the weight of the report, and to address just two points in that respect, at point B of the Prosecution's reply, if Your Honour inspects that paragraph carefully, you will see that in fact those aspects concerning the opportunity to cross-examine an editor and it being insufficient cannot replace the test of whether or not the document is reliable. Those points, again, go back to the Milutinovic dicta concerning admissibility if not weight. Your Honour, reference has also been made to the fact that no examples were given by the Defence in support of the contention that it's often not clear whether a passage of the report is intended to refer to what an individual saw or what an individual was told. With such a weighty tone and having concentrated efforts on other areas, I'd like, however, to direct Your Honours to two examples, one which can be found on page 43 upload in e-court - I'm not going to ask that it be put on the screen now - and another at page 47, English, e-court. Your Honour, in respect of the film, if I can address that briefly, it's my submission that the Prosecution observations within the reply do not address or remedy the essential problem which has been brought to Your Honours' attentions. Namely, that the film lasts for 54 minutes and includes comments from 34 named individuals, some of which remain unnamed. It is claimed that the whole answers of the individuals are included in the film. It's my submission that without the entirety of the footage that made the film, that claim cannot be substantiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. This kind of information is not only missing only here, you would say. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, at the same time, for a full record ... Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a couple of brief comments. I would have to see the footage first in order to comment, but we have provided transcripts to the interpreters if that is of any assistance. We would like to have, of course, a full record, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if something is not in evidence, Ms. Higgins, nevertheless, the record of the proceedings should be complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I therefore give an undertaking that we will provide a transcript of what is seen. It is really is for the purpose of seeing the images. D146 is already in evidence, which is the major portion of this, and, of course, the other part, if Your Honours disagree with my submission, a transcript exists for "Storm Over Croatia," so the compilation of course can be made, and we will undertake to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that it was even part of the -- I remember that I've seen a transcript of -- although not fully read. Ms. Frolich, any objection against the way of proceeding as suggested by Ms. Higgins?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will proceed and, of course, the issue is how to get finally a French text because we are an institution with two official languages --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but we'll resolve that one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, respectfully from the English booth, without the transcript reference, we need to keep up with the subtitles, which will make things impossible for the French booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, we submit that this demonstrates the unreliability of portions of this video that is sought to be admitted, and we would seek a ruling on the admissibility of both the report and the video at this stage of the proceedings. Your Honours will have noted that the overlayed imagery was neither undated -- sorry, was undated and unreferenced as to its location. Your Honour, those conclude my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If I may be allowed just to address a couple of very brief points because I believe the Prosecution's position has been made very clear in the Prosecution reply, Mr. President. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have just as much time as Ms. Higgins has taken. But before we continue, is there anything the other Defence teams would like to add? I see there is no need for that. So Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you for your indulgence, Mr. President. I will still endeavour to be brief. Ms. Higgins has addressed, first and foremost, the point -- really, two points that there is a difference -- that indicia of reliability speak to the admissibility of the report as opposed to the weight that is to be given to the report and to the fact that indicia of reliability that we have provided are not in fact indicia of reliability and that they should not be considered as such by the Chamber. Just at the outset, the issue here is whether this report in these criminal proceedings before this Tribunal is to be admissible and whether the practice of this Tribunal and in particular this Chamber allows it to be admitted into evidence. In that respect, citing a Milutinovic decision and decisions that -- reliance by the Special Court for Sierra Leone we think does not sufficiently prove that -- sufficiently show that the Tribunal's practice is different than this -- or these two decisions, these two Milutinovic decisions, which the Prosecution still believes are rather exceptional. A narrow selection of factors that Ms. Higgins mentions and the broader selection that was chosen by the Milutinovic Chamber, again, do not speak against admission of this report. What is important to show is that there is a prima facie showing of reliability, that there are indicators that only prima facie showing of reliability is required, and the Prosecution indeed showed a number of these indicia that demonstrate this prima facie reliability, which is a very low threshold to be satisfied by a piece of evidence that is to be admitted. Therefore, we think -- the Prosecution still submits that the report possess sufficient indicia as we have shown in our reply, and I do not think that it is necessary that I go over each and every factor. I would just like to address the issue of the self-described role of the Croatian Helsinki Committee for Human Rights in human rights -- in recording and broadcasting human rights abuses. We have in our footnote, in our reply, we have indeed -- we have added the web site of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights to demonstrate that this is an organisation of some merit as is visible from its web site, but we do not confine ourselves to this web site to show the rule of the Helsinki Committee. This is, after all, why we have a witness today who is to testify about its role and its other activities aside from its activities that are related to this report. The indicia of unreliability that Ms. Higgins and, indeed, the Cermak Defence have cited do not necessarily take away, even if they are proven to be true, do not, first of all, take away necessarily from the indicia of reliability that the Prosecution has shown; and we think that it is erroneous to claim that these indicia of reliability do not go to weight to be given to the report but instead to its reliability and, therefore, its admissibility before the Tribunal. As one example, hearsay and no availability for cross-examination of unidentified or inadequately identified individuals or lack of foundation evidence have been found as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: -- factors for -- I am sorry. Maybe I speak a little bit too fast. I apologise to the interpreters and to the Chamber. Maybe have been found to be, indeed, factors that go to weight to be given to a report as cited by the Tribunal practice, and -- which this Chamber has, indeed, endorsed this practice and admitted a number of documents under similar circumstances. When the Prosecution mentioned witnesses Jan Elleby and Mikhail Ermolaev, for example, this -- this example did not only go to show the hearsay evidence as being admissible in such a manner through these two witnesses but also to demonstrate that when there was information recorded in a certain way by certain individuals such as, for example, UNCIVPOL monitors, they were found to be admissible by this Chamber. And in short, we do not believe that it has been sufficiently proven that there are inadequate indicia reliability as to render the report inadmissible. We also think that -- believe that the claim that the aim of the report as well as the aim of the video was a political aim. These are things that are conclusions to be drawn by the Chamber after weighing all relevant evidence that it has admitted, and they -- indeed, any purpose behind the report has -- can only weighed after assessing all available evidence, both that was submitted by the Prosecution and by the Defence. This goes, as I said, both to report and to the video. Claiming that it's a political montage is at this point, especially before hearing the evidence of Witness 140, a very premature assessment and very obviously one-sided assessment. I would like to address the two examples that were given by Ms. Higgins. On pages -- I believe it was at page 41 --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: -- 41 and 45 of the report. I believe, first of all, that questions can be put to Witness 140 whether or not he has any additional knowledge about this incident that might add value to the evidence that is in this report. But in any case, the Prosecution's claim was not to say that each and every fact was described -- each and every piece of evidence described in the report was so clearly described that it would be clear for -- from who the interviewee was and whether this happened to this interviewee or not. It was to say that most instances were clearly shown to be such, that -- in any event, I would submit we should -- the Chamber should defer the decision until the Witness 140 has had a chance to testify. And, finally, as to the video documentary film, storm over Krajina, whereby Ms. Higgins' submitted portions do not assist the Chamber in determining if the video is reliable in its entirety, I would submit that precisely the fact that some portions of this video have been found reliable enough to be admitted by the Chamber goes to show that the entire video possesses sufficient indicia of reliability because of the method of work that the filmmakers have employed in producing this film. The fact that there are overlays, overlaps, and that there's undated pieces, well, the Prosecution was very clear that the primary purpose of this individual is to provide context to the testimony of Witness 140, in particular, his comments that 11 appearances that he makes in the -- during the documentary, which he -- he makes comments that if they were taken out of context, perhaps would not be easily understood; and, more so, even more than just contextual evidence, the Prosecution position is that hearsay evidence, again, goes to weight and not to admissibility of a piece of evidence. This is all I would have to say to -- in reply to Ms. Higgins' comments. I would ask that the Chamber defer its decision on admissibility in the event that it does not reject the Cermak Defence request that it defer its decision on admissibility until after Witness 140 has testified. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few questions, perhaps, and a few attempts to clarify matters. I understood Ms. Higgins to say that the Milutinovic decision was part of pleadings before the Court of Sierra Leone, rather than that they were adopted by the Sierra Leone Court, as I understood you, Ms. Higgins; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct, and it's a Defence response to an application to have NGO documents submitted, which is still pending before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if it pleaded before the magistrate court in Dublin or before any -- I mean, putting -- making it an argument before another court, does that in itself add anything to what apparently is the convincing argument of the decision itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Firstly, I'd make two points, the first point being, the fact that it may be a different or lesser-used approach described as exceptional may or may not be correct. If it is correct, that assessment that it is it exceptional, doesn't necessarily mean that it's wrong because once one considers that decision one will see that it was a thoroughly reasoned decision giving specific detail and specific consideration to the content of the entirety of the report. The second appointment I would make is this, in relation to the fact that it has been pleaded before the Special Court of Sierra Leone. Defence counsel in that case obviously took a view about the strength of the decision itself and whether or not it was legitimate to rely upon that decision in trying to persuade the Court also to follow the Milutinovic route. I do not say and do not wish to try and assess what the Chamber in that court will do, but it is an approach, an approach which is being used and relied upon. I go no further than that. But I submit that it was relevant for this Chamber to know about the frequency with which that decision sought to be relied upon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. Ms. Frolich, listening to you, I got the impression that you either did not fully understand what Ms. Higgins was saying or that did you not wish to understand it. Where you said that portions of what we find in the video are admitted into evidence, so therefore reliable enough to consider the whole of the video, now, the argument, if I analyse it, it means as long as there are reliable portions in the video, you can mix it up with whatever you want because that would justify admission into evidence of the whole of the video with whatever you have mixed it up. Is that your argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The argument that I was trying to make - perhaps I was not successful - was if there reliable portions, that adds to the likelihood that the remainder of the video is reliable. But I think that it is clear from the video what has been edited and what has not, and it's clear to the Chamber what conclusions it can draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think Ms. Higgins showed us this specific portion because apparently she has concerns about combining a statement by one of the accused on video, to combine that with the images of people who apparently have -- at least are not shown on this picture to have freedom of movement, packed in a rather small room, I think the concern of Ms. Higgins is that she says, This is biased information because there is a clear suggestion that what the person speaking says is lip service to what doesn't exist in reality, where Ms. Higgins says, I don't know whether you've taken these pictures from. Was it at the same time? Was it half a year before? Is it in Bosnia? Is it in -- I think that's her major concern, and to say, well, to show these together, that -- and you have not -- at least not clearly addressed that concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I do understand this concern. I -- I do agree with Ms. Higgins. I can agree fully with that concern. Again, I would reiterate the position that it is clear what is what in the video because it is it clear from the images shown that the images are not part of the interview that General Cermak gave, and it is clear that, also from the images shown, they are undated. Therefore, what weight can be given to this particular set of images is up to the Chamber to decide. I can -- I can certainly agree that very little weight can be attached to such images. I do not think that takes away from showing the interview that General Cermak gave, for example, or the entire context of the video that is shown as a -- the video that is it shown as context to the evidence of Witness 140, and, again, I believe that Witness 140 can provide more details about this video and whether his own statements were taken out of context or not, which is what the Prosecution is concerned with the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Finally, is it your intention to play the whole video in court, or are we just supposed to look at it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We do not want to waste the Chamber's time unless the Chamber so pleases. The video lasts 50 minutes. We thought it might be a little too long unless the Chamber is so inclined, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's not a matter of taking the Chamber's time but whether to take courtroom time because the Chamber would have to look at it anyhow. Unless we would immediately now, on the basis of Ms. Higgins's submissions, decide that it's excluded. Yes, I don't want to make this -- and I think the positions are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have an early break so that the Chamber is in a position to consider the matter. We will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the various submissions, in relation to the report, Military Operation Storm and Its Aftermath, and the video. As far as the video is concerned, the Chamber defers its decision on admission and, at the same time, is aware that this might cause you some problems as far as cross-examination is concerned. One of the reasons to defer the decision is that the Chamber feels unable to finally decide the matter on the basis of just a portion shown to it. At the same time - and I'm now speaking for myself, and I know this is if not for the full 100 percent then at least for a large percentage true for my colleague - is that knowing that, Ms. Higgins, that you would like to make submissions on the matter, I refrain from looking at the video at all, so I have not seen any further than what you have showed us, and that's usually not the case. If statements or videos are submitted to the Chamber, we usually look at it, but we have -- at least I'm speaking now for myself, but again, from what I know, it's mainly true for my colleagues, as well, that we refrained from first gaining an impression before having listened to you. That also means that since the Chamber, of course, then will have to look at that we hope to give a decision by tomorrow morning when we have reviewed the video as a whole, which might accommodate some of the concerns for cross-examination. Ms. Frolich, the Chamber understands that you didn't wish to play it, so I don't think that apart from the abstract, no reference will be made to the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: The intention was to play a few minutes of the video to put some of the comments of the witness in context as I was going through my direct examination, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then, it will be MFI'd of course, whatever the witness says.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's found that the video would not be admitted into evidence, then we still could consider whether or not that small portion - I don't know what it is - whether there would be objection against admission of that small portion as well. We'll then wait and see. Now I turn to the report. With respect to the report, the report Military Operation Storm and Its Aftermath, the Chamber has decided that it will consider the report for admission but only in part. Not considered for admission are part 2 of the report, which is devoted exclusively to Sector North; and also not considered for admission are any statements purportedly made or represented to have been made by any of the accused. Now, the non-admission of the part of the report containing statements purportedly made or represented to have been made by any of the accused shall not prevent the Prosecution from seeking to elicit evidence on what apparently is described in the report from the witness, but then, of course, it would be required to lay a foundation as to the source of knowledge of the witness. Where statements made in the report or information given in the report makes reference to both Sector South and Sector North, in such cases, the statements made or the information given as to Sector North shall be handled by the Chamber similarly to its approach to part 2 of the report. The Chamber further wishes to make clear two matters to the parties; first, that any eventual admission decision as to the remaining parts of the report - the parts not yet excluded - does not mean that the Chamber will accept any conclusions made or reached in the report; and the Chamber further wants to make clear that it will be critical of any conclusions so made or reached in the report when drawing its own conclusions on the basis of the totality of the evidence. The parties may proceed and examine the witness as to the report in line with the guidance here given; and, finally, the Prosecution is invited to already start preparing for redactions in line with the guidance hereby given. Ms. Frolich, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President. The Prosecution is ready and calls Witness 140, Professor Zarko Puhovski. Mr. President, if I can just briefly address the Chamber before the witness comes in, just in relation to the part of the Chamber's decision where it said that you would not consider Sector North for part -- part 2, Sector North, for admission. I would just like to clarify that the witness in proofing clarified to the Prosecution that the portion of the report that he wrote was not in fact as previously stated by the witness the conclusion to Sector South part, first part of the report, but introductory part to the second part, and this was an error on his part, and I do not wish to pre-empt the witness testimony, but this part which he wrote which relates to both Sector North and Sector South is in fact located in the beginning of part 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be clear to you, Ms. Frolich, that the Chamber doesn't want to cross the borders of the indictment, and if the witness can tell us more about what happened across those borders, the Chamber is not interested -- interested at this moment in hearing of this. But -- one second. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Puhovski, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed it out you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhovski. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, we are just dealing with a procedural matter, although not unrelated to your testimony. If you would just allow the Chamber to continue for a second. Ms. Frolich, is it clear what inspired the Chamber to do this, and if the witness would know a lot about what has happened in another part of the world, I mean, it's a matter of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. President. I wanted to point out the fact that -- of course, the Chamber would have to look at this, but the part that the witness in fact wrote did relate to Sector South part of the report as well. It was just located in a different place, which the witness can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the reasoning behind the -- I would say provisional ruling because what we said is we decided not to consider. We said something about a mixture North and South elsewhere in the report, if there would be relevant material for Sector South in part 2, which now apparently would be within direct knowledge of the witness. You may address that, and, of course, we'll deal with the matter on the basis of what I think everyone understood was our decision not to spend time on irrelevant geographical parts. If you would please keep that in mind, then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Zarko Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What is your occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm a professor at the Faculty of Philosophy at the Zagreb University.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What was your occupation during the period from 1993 to 1998 and 2000 to 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: In the earlier period, I was a member and deputy president; and in the latter period, the president of the Croatian Human Rights Committee, Helsinki Watch -- Helsinki Committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 13th and 14th June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we have -- sorry, Mr. Registrar, could we have 65 ter 6798 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, do you see the first page of this document that Mr. Registrar is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on 13 and 14 June 2007 and signed by you at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you also provide information to the Office of the Prosecutor that was put in a supplemental information sheet on 18 December 2008 and 9th and 11th February, 2009?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we have 65 ter 7152 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Is this the supplemental information sheet that you provided on 18th December, 2008, and 9th/11th February, 2009, which you signed at the bottom, and --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, save for the fact that I think it says 2008, and it must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What year should it be?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: It should be 2009 -- 2008 instead of 2009. 1008

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1008 seems to be quite in the past. If you wouldn't mind -- well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quite old but not that old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 18th of December, to say, 2009 sounds not correct to me because that's in the future. Ms. Frolich, was the supplemental information sheet prepared both six weeks ago and a couple of days ago?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Some information was put together on the 18th December, and then continuation was -- continued proofing was done on 9th and 11th February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of this year?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: This year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'm now still -- oh, yes, I see. It's not the date at the top, but it's the date further down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There I see. Yes, I think obvious mistakes do not need to be clarified. It is on the record that the 18th December is a reference to 6 weeks ago and not to 1.000 years and 6 weeks ago. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, after both your statements that we have just seen were recorded, were they read back to you in the language you understand, or did you have a chance to read them in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I read them myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When read to you, did the statements accurately reflect what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review both the original statement from 2007 and the supplemental information sheet, again, in the language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Were these two statements in full accordance with the truth as you know it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Would you give the same statement today if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, could both the 65 ter 6798 and 7152 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we know by now is there was an objection against paragraph 14 and 15 of the statement of 2007 where reference is made to the report. The Chamber is not aware of the position taken by Defence counsel on the supplemental information sheet. Could I hear whether there is any objection against admission of the supplemental information sheet?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the supplemental information sheet, in fact, two were served, and I'm currently in the process of trying to reconcile the differences between the two of them. So primarily, Your Honour, I would ask, perhaps, that they be marked for identification until I can make a final determination for my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll assign numbers, first of all, to 6798, the 2007 statement. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2316. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2316 is marked for identification. A decision on admission will follow most likely together with the decision on the report. Then 65 ter 7152, supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P2317, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And once you have resolved the problem, of course - the Chamber is unaware of because we have only received one supplemental information sheet - would you please let us know. I took it, since I did not hear from other Defence counsel, that they joined the submissions made by Ms. Higgins, and that is now confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this point I would like to seek your permission to add two documents that are not on the 65 ter list presently, which are provisionally signed 65 ter numbers 7148 and 7150 to 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the first document that's cited 7148, I have an objection as to its admissibility, but I know that Your Honours are concerning initially the 65 ter issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Which I have no observations on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the same is true for 7150, 65 ter? No observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then leave is granted to add 65 ter 7148 and 7150 to the 65 ter list, and this is not a decision on admission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to read the summary of witness evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Zarko Puhovski was a member of the Croatian Helsinki Committee for Human Rights from its inception in 1993 to 1998 and from 2000 to 2007 when he became its chairperson. The witness describes the role of the Croatian Helsinki --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: -- its procedure for recording human rights abuses and compiling reports of these abuses; its fact-finding missions to the Krajina in 1995. The witness also describes -- sorry, I was receiving French translation for a moment. The witness also describes the political climate and actors in Croatia in 1995. The witness edited the Croatian Helsinki Committee report, Military Operation Storm and Its Aftermath, which details human rights violations in Sectors North and Sector South in Croatia during and after Operation Storm. Information contained in Croatian Helsinki Committee report was disseminated to the Croatian authorities. Croatian officials denied crimes happened or denied responsibility for these crimes. The witness describes how the Croatian Helsinki Committee created its lists of missing and killed and in particular that it would only place a name of a killed person on such a list if it was confirmed by two independent sources. Information was also corroborated by other NGOs and Helsinki Committee offices in the region. Finally, the witness describes his visit to Knin in August 1995, including his observations during that visit. According to the witness, no comprehensive or competent investigation was carried out by the Croatian authorities into crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm. That concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, could you please describe the role of the Croatian Helsinki Committee in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: The Croatian Helsinki Committee was set up in late March 1993. It consisted of 22, 30 mostly well-known and well reputed public persons from Croatian society; artists, politicians, and so on and so forth. It had been 20 and 25 employees who, when our financial situation was better, had duties to discharge in the office in Osijek, later on in Vukovar, Karlovac, later on in Knin, Dubrovnik, as well as in the central office in Zagreb. The office dealt with the promotion of human rights and the analysis of the situation with regard to the exercise of human rights. Many citizens of Serb ethnicity contacted us who believed that their rights were threatened. On average, 2.000 individuals would approach us every year, and the absolute majority of them was of Croatian ethnic origin, but there were the Serbs and the Roma present in the percentages as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could you describe what the status of the Croatian Helsinki Committee was as an organisation in Croatia, under Croatian law?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: We were a non-governmental organisation, initially set up under a piece of legislation that remained from the former system as a representative of a foreign organisation, that's to say the international Helsinki organisation, and later on as a Croatian organisation as well. Legally speaking -- or, rather, for several years we were an organisation that was subject to many attacks because it was believed that we were more concerned with the rights of the Serbs in Croatia rather than the Croats, and there are over a hundred articles and broadcasts of political functionaries attacking us. Our activists were under attack, as well, but the situation began settling down and calming down towards 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Why do you think the Croatian Helsinki Committee was being attacked in the years that you talk about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Because the committee was outside of what you would term the mainstream, that's to say, the prevalent political line in Croatia; because it represented the rights of those who -- whose rights were not even referred to as rights and could therefore not be considered to have been violated either; or the individuals, the violation of whose rights had to be tacitly ignored because it was believed that in times of war the insistence of rights of some, like, for instance, the members of the Serb minority, could endanger or aggravate the position of Croatia in war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What, if any, political affiliations did the organisation have or does still have today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: No. The members of the organisation were individuals of different religious, political, and other convictions, but under the statute of the international Helsinki organisation, it was not allowed to have any political affiliations in terms of membership of the political parties or liaisons or connections with the bodies of any state.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What, if any, other types of association did -- or does the Croatian Helsinki Committee have? Other types of associations.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What, if any, other groups in Croatia or abroad did the Croatian Helsinki Committee work with or does work with?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: The Croatian Helsinki Committee primarily cooperated with the Helsinki Committee or the organisations similar to it by nature in Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina; there were two in Kosovo and Macedonia as well; then with the fund for humanitarian law led by Madam Natasa Kandic, and with a number of non-governmental organisations in Croatia such as the Civic Committee for Human Rights and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Now, Professor Puhovski, how well did you know Petar Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpretation was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Who is Petar Mrkalj -- who was Petar Mrkalj, and how well did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I knew Petar Mrkalj well for almost the last 20 years of his life. He was an associate of the Croatian Helsinki Committee ever since its inception, and from 1994 his executive manager, the person who was in charge of -- he was a person who was in charge of the staff in the Croatian Helsinki Committee. Previously, I knew him as a journalist from Karlovac who was a prominent figure on the trade union scene in the last years of Yugoslavia, which had experienced a sort of liberalisation, and some sort of social and political action could be witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In paragraphs 2 and 3 of your supplemental information sheet, which is P2317 MFI, you mentioned other members of the fact-finding team. Did you know these people personally?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me just say that I don't have this version of the report with me here. Of course, I knew the people who were involved in the making of the report because I was the deputy president of the committee they worked for. All of them were individuals who had professionally been working for the Croatian Helsinki Committee in either Zagreb, Karlovac, or Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: With the Chamber's leave, if we have hard copies of the witness's statements, if Madam Usher could provide them to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to paragraph 6 of your supplemental information sheet, which is the document you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor yesterday, and ask you how and when did you learn of the methodology that was used to collect the information on fact-finding missions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: To put it simply, we learned as we went along how we should go about things. We had only members of the committee. We didn't even have an office at the time. We were given a small office area of some 30 square metres. Then we got a bigger office, and gradually we employed people. From the start, it would so happen that initially dozens and later on hundreds and thousands of people would approach us, seeking to have their rights honoured, and as -- people gained experience. As of autumn 1994, we organised in-house, weekend seminars together with some other non-governmental organisations from Zagreb and elsewhere where, together with the people from the International Helsinki Federation and the ICRC as well as some of our colleagues from the faculty of law, we engaged in the effort of training our men, primarily in the fields of gathering information, report-writing. The aim was to make sure that the reports are written as objectively as possible and as quickly as possible and that every single fact is verified and double-checked. We had three to four seminars of this sort, which had as their purpose, also, the exchange of experience. The attendees of the seminars who were members of these various organisations had already had several years of experience by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. That was going to be one of my next questions. I, however, have in mind something more specific. When in paragraph 6 you mention when the team members, so of the -- I believe that you should take a look at paragraph 6 of the supplemental information sheet that you provided to the office recently. And you mentioned that when teams returned from mission, you said, I quote: "Either Ivan Zvonimir Cicak ..." or you, "... would talk to the team members about the mission details in debriefings." Could you describe these debriefings in more detail?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: This was roughly the procedure. A team of some two to three individuals would go into -- to visit a couple of villages in close proximity of each other for a couple of days. Thereupon, they would go back to Zagreb, write an initial version of the report and submit it to Petar Mrkalj, who was in charge of the entire team. Several days later, Petar Mrkalj would organise their meeting with either Mr. Cicak, who was the president of the committee at the time, or with me - I was the deputy president chairman at the time - rarely with both of us, where they would present their observations to us. We had already received a hand-written version of the report by that time. We would also have occasion to see the photographs that they would bring along with them, and very often we would also listen to the audiotapes of the statements taken from eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Other than information that was provided to you by the team members, was there any other -- what other source, if any, did you have of information that was presented to you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: As a committee, we used all possible information we could get by, using media information that we tried to verify, official positions of governmental functionaries, documents of the UN, the ICRC, as well as documents of other NGOs. We also used information received from journalists who happened to be in certain locations. For example, in the case of Varivode, we received information from a Czech TV crew which happened to be there. Varivode is the place where a month and a half after the operation, a grave crime occurred. Also, we kept having people appearing at the office to volunteer, bringing in information, which in turn needed to be checked. Frequently, those people were under a lot of pressure, emotional pressure, and not everything they said to us could be taken for granted. In any case, we took all of those factors into account, be it in terms of which locations to go or to try to corroborate that through the facts obtained by our volunteers while visiting certain locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 7 of the same statement, you mentioned that Mr. Mrkalj was afraid that something would happen to the material. And what -- do you know why he was afraid, and would you say his fears were justified?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, he mentioned that back in 1995 and 1996. I frequently mocked him, and I told him he was paranoid. But it was subsequently proven that the secret service of the Ministry of Defence launched an operation under the Code name of "Chameleon." Their task to penetrate the Croatian Helsinki Committee. They recruited one of our employees, and they wanted to get by as much information and documents we had as possible. In 2001, I was president of the HHO, and the then executive director, Mr. Gazivoda, was summoned to come to the Ministry of Defence in order for them to show us all those documents because the operation became publicly known by that time and some of their staff disciplined. They had a number of documents, including hand-written notes which were kept during meetings and exchanged among us and then discarded. To put it in a different way, unfortunately, Mr. Mrkalj seems to have been right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you know why this operation took place and why your offices were searched and documents copied?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, going through the information of those who were disciplined for carrying out that operation, their justification was that we monitored the movements and tactics of the Croatian army, and they believed we were a legitimate target for such an investigation by an MOD service.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, if I could turn to drafting of the report which you mention in paragraph 14 of your 2007 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: That's 2316.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Report, Military Operation Storm and Its Aftermath. That was, as you say, written by Mr. Mrkalj. You say you wrote the conclusion for the version published in the form of a book in 2001. Could you clarify what you meant by this conclusion that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: The final report resulting from all the field investigation came about in 1999, while I was in charge of a graduate course in Austria and was not actively participating in the work of the Croatian Helsinki Committee. The report was completed by Mr. Mrkalj. That version together with the photographs was distributed in some 150 copies to all important state institutions, the media, as well as foreign missions in Zagreb. Upon my return to the Croatian Helsinki Committee in the summer of 2001, we managed to receive financial support from the Norwegian Helsinki Committee and the Nieman Foundation to publish that report in the form of a book. On that occasion, I drafted the text following a request of the executive council of the Croatian Helsinki Committee. I drafted that on the fifth anniversary of Operation Storm. It was made public as a statement of the Croatian Helsinki Committee in August 2000. We added that to the second part of the book, since the first one was already being edited, and for financial reasons, we completed, first, the part which had to do with the south, and then what followed was another part that had to do with Sector North. My text appeared as an introduction to the Sector North part, and prior to the publishing of the book we were distributing our report on Sector North by way of photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you recall what were your main points from this introduction, in fact? What did you write about in this introduction?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: In the introduction, I basically wrote that five years back, looking at the operation, it was necessary to mention the reasons for it, and we believed it to be necessary from the point of view of human rights. First and foremost, it eliminated something called the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was founded on a systematic denial of human rights of all those inhabiting it, as well as carrying out attacks along its borders into the Croatian territory and cutting off road communication. The text was officially adopted by our council, and in it I also cautioned that that operation brought about a result of its own in which there was serious violations of human rights, resulting in several hundreds of deaths, and I also mentioned that a great many people had to leave their homes. Basically, the effect of the operation was equal to that of an ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And did this introduction relate to Sector North, Sector South, or both?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: It had to do with both Sectors. It was the official position of the Croatian Helsinki Committee on the fifth anniversary of the operation we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we show 65 ter 4674, first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, I take it that this is the report, the book report that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that is the book. I have a copy here, as well, in the Croatian language. The one with the red cover is the English version of the same book.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And both were -- both versions were produced by Croatian Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we go to page 206 in e-court in English and page 194 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, is this the introduction that we have just discussed, that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: However, this is page 193.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: We are -- the electronic versions of pages are different. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: In the book it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. What was the basis for -- you state certain conclusions in this introduction. What was the basis for your conclusions that you set out in this introduction?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Based on the report, since I double-checked the text prior to the publication of the book, and based on the fact that we were still receiving reports of many who were talking about what they went through or their neighbours or members of their families, and based on the reports we received from our colleagues in Belgrade and Bijeljina, where there was the Helsinki Committee in charge of Republika Srpska, and based on the interviews of my work-mates from the Helsinki Committee on their own experience in the period between 1995 and 2000, it all served as the basis of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, I'm working on the basis of the book as attached to your submission, so therefore, I would be greatly assisted if you would point at the pages numbering as we find them in the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: This is page -- in English, page 0610-1821, and I -- that's the ERN number. Now, if -- if you would just allow me a moment to find the pages in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I found it more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: The page is 193 in B/C/S and 205 in English in hard copy, although the page number is not visible on the first page of the actual introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I had the introduction for part 2, pages 105 to 205, and now we're taken to -- and I'm looking at the hard copy pages. So I'm really lost about six or seven kinds of numbering of ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could also point out more confusion. The P2317, which is the supplemental sheet, at paragraph 18 says that the conclusion is pages 135 to 136 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes. We have informed Defence counsel in an e-mail yesterday of additional changes that were made by the witness after the finalisation of the proofing note. Since it was so late, the only recourse we had was to send an e-mail to the Defence counsel saying that the conclusion that he talks about in the supplemental information sheet is in fact an introduction which is, of course, located on different pages of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We try to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My confusion is I don't think he -- I could be wrong, but he corrected that, or was this corrected when he now gave the 92 ter declarations?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Ms. Frolich, as I said before, we don't usually have 65 ter documents, et cetera, so I worked on the basis of the copy that was provided to us as an attachment to the motion. Now, what I see is that in the table of contents, the introduction goes from page 105 to 205. 205 starts with Military Police Operation Storm, the first chapter of part 2. Now, the page numbering in the hard copy is not consistent with the table of contents. Apparently, part 1 ends page 208. So the numbering on the copy we received is incomplete, and now I do understand that you took us to page 205, which is called: Introduction, Presumptions For Facing the Past.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do not see any such chapter in the table of content, or do I?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I believe that the table of contents is slightly misleading because in fact the introduction is located on page 205 in hard copy, so that is all I can say on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whereas the table of contents says that the introduction is to be found on page ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I see that the introduction takes a couple of pages in the book --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and where in the table of contents it takes a hundred pages, nothing in relation to what we find then on the other pages. I'm really confused about -- could you take us always to the pages in the hard copy, and I'll forget about the table of contents. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President. This is, therefore -- the page in hardcopy is 205 in English version, and that is - I repeat the ERN number - 0610-1821, and it goes until page 208, and that's ERN 0610-1824, and that is what is being shown in e-court, so I think that at least that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem if we follow it in e-court, the minute that you are dealing with another matter, it has disappeared, whereas sometimes I want to use my own material. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I would like to take you on page --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: This is page 207 in English, and in e-court this is page 208, so I was referring to the hard copy page first. In e-court, this is page 208, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your -- you list reasons why the action should be evaluated negatively, and you mentioned some of it before. Could I ask you to comment on subparagraph (e): "The government's decision to institute organised occupation of the flats and houses of expelled inhabitants." What did you mean by this comment, and how did you come to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: After the operation ended, among the public, the general belief was that things were over and that the people who had left that part of Croatia, who were mostly Serbs, would never return. Croatian citizens of Croatian ethnic background who had been expelled from Bosnia-Herzegovina from those parts under control of the regime of Republika Srpska received in hundreds of cases, and even more, written certificates or approvals of local authorities, enabling them to move into the houses of those ethnic Serbs who had left them. In other words, those people were not robbers, people breaking into others' apartments and houses. They had documents for which they rightly believed were valid. The local authorities were distributing those in agreement with the Croatian governmental bodies, especially following the decision that property rights temporarily be suspended in that part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: In the period between the fall of 1995 and the fall of 1997, we had reports of over 200 people who tried to go back to Croatia and into their houses. They found people there who for the most part were ethnic Croats, Croatian citizens who had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, and who literally displayed approvals for them to reside in those houses. There was much litigation, many cases; I believe some are still pending before certain courts. Many of them were resolved after a number of years only.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: May I just -- for the sake of clarification, what you just said is in English is: "They found people there who for the most part were ethnic Croats, Croatian citizens who had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, and who literally displayed approvals for them to reside in those houses." Could you clarify, who was -- who were the ethnic Croats, persons who tried to go back to Croatia, or persons who had approvals to reside in houses, if that is clear to you.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Those people who wanted to return were ethnic Serbs of Croatian citizenship. They wanted to return once it was made possible with the things slowly beginning to normalize in terms of relations between Croatia and the FRY. They wanted to return to their former homes. In those homes, they came upon new inhabitants who, without exception, basically, were ethnic Croats of Croatian citizenship who had been forced to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. Formally speaking, it was an ethnic issue. However, the authorities used the logic that most ethnic Serbs of Croatian citizenship who had left Croatia in the summer of 1995 would never return. That is why they put those homes at the disposal of other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, you have -- as you stated, you have read the report, you have edited the report, and this report contains a lot of conclusions. Do you know what basis, first of all, existed for making those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Most of the conclusions are based on the reports of the teams comprised of those working for the Croatian Helsinki Committee who toured certain villages, hamlets, and towns in those parts of Croatia where there were war activities in August 1995. Some of the conclusions are based on general information from the media and those provided by the authorities, as well as reports of international organisations, including the ICRC, as well as the reports of NGOs from Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps I shouldn't say Serbia, but what was then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
