utterances.text: Did you personally agree with the conclusions that are set out in the report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I stand by all of the conclusions in general. There are certain sentences or statements that I may disagree with, but it wasn't my role as deputy president of the Croatian Helsinki Committee to censure or change the views of those working for the committee and those of Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Mrkalj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, however, insist that certain formulations be changed, whereas most of them remained untouched. All of those were included in the body of text that we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now what -- could you give us examples of such formulations that you did not agree with?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: In all of my discussions with the colleagues who had worked on the report, I stood by an old rule for all journalists, which goes something along the lines of: We want nouns and verbs rather than adjectives. Whenever possible, I crossed out all adjectives from the report because I thought adjectives are not something that is needed in such a report, that facts alone suffice. For example, I remember of the instance of cruel murders being referred to in the report. I often stated that we were not the judiciary and that we were not to state between more or less cruel murders but to talk about murders, full stop. On the other hand, parts of the reports which had been drafted in its original version in early 1998 contained the feeling of heated debate, which existed in Croatia on both sides at the time. Some of the formulations were rather sharp and heavy on the part of certain politicians and governmental representatives being directed at Croatian Helsinki Committee workers. For example, a person from Zadar stated that our colleagues laughed out loud when they entered Varivode, seeing all the victims there, because that would give them some ammunition to further attack Croatia. That person was not in Varivode at all, but this only shows the nature of attacks we were exposed to. Some such statements and reactions were not appropriate, in my view. However, some of them remain in the report still. I still believe that our basic intention and goal was to present facts and that the basic formulations had to remain as originally put down by Mr. Mrkalj or some of the other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Just as a matter of reference, this incident is described on page 57 -- hard copy page 57 of the English version. I unfortunately do not have the e-court page. That's 0610-1673, bottom of the page. Could we go to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add just one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: At page 63 of the Croatian hard copy, there is one formulation to be found, which -- or, rather, a paragraph which I subsequently added, which has the title "Graveyards," and I'm referring to the paragraph which follows the title, and it speaks of the fact that many victims could not be avoided when these civilians and soldiers were killed, and it was stated that primarily what we were concerned with were the victims and the families of these victims who had gone through the plight. That was our major concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I believe this is page 65 in English hard copy, ERN 0610-1681. Again, I don't have an e-court page with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, what did you know about position of General Cermak in 1995 during and after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: That's it, precisely what we have on our screens now. I -- my knowledge came from three sources. Our colleagues would always come back from field work with the stories where they would tell us that the political functionaries, those of them who wanted to speak to them, would always answer by saying, We have to ask or consult with General Cermak first. When I was in Knin, I spoke to Mr. Petar Pasic who, on several occasions told me that it was General Cermak who decided on all the important matters. Thirdly, I also present the viewpoint of General Cervenko in this report, who as a commander had to have known about these matters and who speaks very clearly of the position of General Cermak, the way all of us perceived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to interrupt, but Your Honour has made a ruling concerning statements made by the accused, first of all, and I would seek to agree with Ms. Frolich at which parts link to Your Honours' ruling in consistency with what remains in the report because there are many sections, that being one of them, which I would seek to challenge. If I couldn't agree with Ms. Frolich, Your Honour, I would seek a ruling from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm understood correctly Ms. Higgins. Does it mean if she had in mind all portions of the report that deal with General Cermak in any way, or just those portions that -- that the witness will comment on, if I show portions of the report to the witness or ... I do not quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, I think that the ruling or the guidance given portions not to be considered for admission were statements purportedly made or represented to have been made by the accused, that this were the accused speak. At the same time, the ruling included that we would not accept that -- we would not admit that as -- those portions of the report and, at the same time, that the Prosecution could elicit such evidence from the witness after they had laid a foundation on what the -- what the source of knowledge would be. So we'll not just accept it from the report, saying, This is what happened during the meeting; but if Ms. Frolich wants to elicit from the witness asking him what happened on that day, how do you know, who told you, were you present, et cetera, then we would consider such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful, and I will perhaps save my reservations for references to the report itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And to the extent this is not clear, I could try to take you back to the relevant portion of where I gave the guidance but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I have that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, you mention in your statement, you mentioned the -- that members of the Croatian Helsinki Committee participated in a mission with the members of the International Helsinki Federation and that they visited Krajina and Knin during that time. What do you know of their visit and their mission to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Immediately after the action was finished, we received first information that at that time was fully unreliable and unverified. Still, they pointed to some suspected events, and we informed our colleagues at home and also our colleagues in Vienna. In view of the situation as it existed at the time at the end of the operation, and in view of the pressure under which the Croatian Helsinki Committee had to work, we believed it would be appropriate for some of our international colleagues to come to Croatia and see what the situation was like. The mission spent some two days in the field together with our colleagues, and they held a press conference on the 22nd of August, unless I'm mistaken, where the first findings of the mission were presented. I remember going to Knin one day to check if they would be able to reach Knin at all, and that was the extent of my connection with the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you know of a visit of the team members of the International Helsinki Federation with Croatian Helsinki Committee to General Cermak in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Basically what was published in the report and what was published at the press conference. Therefore, only second-hand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has ruled that on these kind of meetings where Mr. Cermak is presented as what he said, et cetera, that we'll not rely on the report. So we just forget about what the report says in this respect. Could you please give details, Ms. Frolich, as to how you learned about a meeting taking place at all, what you know about those who were present -- well, so Ms. Frolich will explore with you the sources of your knowledge of the meeting and what was said during that meeting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I heard. When the colleagues came back from Knin, I talked to them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you already. You're talking about colleagues coming back from Knin. Could you tell us who you are talking about. Who were these colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gashi and Mr. Hayden from the International Helsinki Federation and Petra Klein and Petar Mrkalj from the Croatian Helsinki Committee who were on the team with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did they return from a meeting you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They returned from a 2-day stay at Knin at which time, they had, as they told me, a meeting with Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you remember what point in time that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At what point in time during their stay in Knin, unfortunately, I don't know. I only know that over the two days that they spent in the area they spoke to General Cermak. That's the extent of what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the two days were what dates, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been the 15th and the 16th of August, unless I'm mistaken, of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they tell you whether one of them or more of them had been present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All four of them were, to my knowledge. All four of them attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when they told you about this meeting, who was telling the story? Was it all four of them or everyone, in bits and pieces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Primarily Mr. Gashi. Mr. Mrkalj and Mrs. Klein were our associates with whom I could have been in contact otherwise, whereas Mr. Gashi and Mr. Hayden left Zagreb the following day, and they were the ones I spoke to most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the other two were present when Mr. Gashi told you about the meeting. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All four of them were present at the meeting, plus two more associates of the Croatian Helsinki Committee who stayed back in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were seven people altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seven, yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Gashi told you about this meeting and what had happened, did any of the others who were present at the time and, as you said, you thought they had been present during this meeting with Mr. Cermak, as well, did they ever intervene or correct Mr. Gashi in what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I don't remember all the details. But basically the difference was that Mr. Mrkalj, our director, Mr. Petar Mrkalj believed that Mr. Gashi portrayed the atmosphere at the meeting in a more sanitized way because Mr. Mrkalj had felt the meeting was more uncomfortable than had been portrayed by Mr. Gashi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they tell you what language was used during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, Mrs. Petra Klein interpreted at all the meetings, including that one. In other words they spoke English, and Ms. Petra Klein interpreted for them, that's to say from English to Croatian back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and what Mr. Cermak would have said would have been translated by her, as well, as far as you know, into English again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, may I take it that some members of -- some who were present during this meeting would have directly understood the words spoken by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Ms. Petra Klein understood both language. Mr. Mrkalj understood Croatian and -- sorry, Mr. Gashi, who is an Albanian, who understood pretty well Croatian and English, and Mr. Hayden understood only English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when they reported to you in this meeting in Zagreb, what language was used then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Klein was interpreting for Mr. Mrkalj with -- through Chuchutage by whispering into his ear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do I then understand that Mr. Gashi, who reported to you, had a reasonable knowledge of the Croatian language which allowed him to directly understand what Mr. Cermak may have said in Knin, and that he reported to you in English? You understand fairly well English, may I take it? I see you nodding yes, which is now on the record. Which was, at the same time, translated into Croatian for those who didn't understand English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only Mr. Mrkalj who did not understand English at this meeting that we had, whereas Mr. Gashi spoke English for the sake of Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I leave it in the hands of Ms. Frolich to -- if she wishes to do so, to ask further questions what exactly was reported in relation to that meeting that had taken place in Knin. Please proceed, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: So, Professor Puhovski, do you recall what was said to you as -- what was reported to you as said in the meeting with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Basically, Mr. Gashi said that they had been received well and that Mr. Cermak either tried to minimise what they presented as the data or suspicions about crime having been committed; whereas Mr. Mrkalj did not believe that they were particularly well received and that Mr. Cermak said things which Petar Mrkalj said at the time were not true. I repeat, Mr. Gashi was quite cautious at the time. He believed that Mr. Cermak stated that he had that knowledge, that he knew what was going on, and at the end he said that he would make sure that such things did not happen anymore and that he would make sure that investigations are -- were carried out into the matter, whereas the opinion of Mr. Mrkalj was that this was purely a phrase to finish off the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Would be able to recall any exact words or phrases that were spoken in that meeting and that were relayed to you, and on what subject matter specifically?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Unfortunately, so many years later, I can't recall the exact words. What I can recall is that the discussion had to do with the preliminary information we had at the -- our disposal at the time, and these were several dozens of people killed or missing. We also discussed the fact that the situations involving first looting and then torching continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, I see -- you told us in your previous answer that you received the report on whether Mr. Cermak had knowledge of what was going on, and in the next sentence you used the phrase that he would take care that such things would not further happen. Could you be more concrete as what you referred to, what was going on, and what such things were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was beyond dispute when everybody's concerned that after Operation Storm, the instances of looting and torching occurred. What was being discussed, and it had to do with the future, in the conversation with Mr. Cermak was that further looting and torching would be prevented. Nobody even expected it necessary to speak of the need to prevent further murders because nobody expected that murders would be committed in the future. Whatever had to do with the future had to do with - to put it this way - discipline, the prevention of individuals going out into villages, looting and torching. This is what the part of the conversation which had to do with the future dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it where in your next answer you talked about murders, looting and torching, that only looting and torching were reported to you as having been the subject of discussion in Knin, whereas the murder was not dealt with in the expectation that there would be no further murders? Is that correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When discussing the future. Based on the report I received, Mr. Cermak practically refused to speak of murders, in plural, and he could not even be saying that such things would not happen anymore because he said that such things had not happened. There were several isolated instances of it, and he could not have been talking about such things not happening again. What was being discussed was the looting and torching, and this was something that was discussed in the context of the future. This is something that both Mr. Gashi and Mr. Mrkalj told me, which was that Mr. Cermak said that the information about the larger numbers of civilians having been killed were not true. Once he reacted in this way, he responded to the information they gave him in this way, they could not have ensued any more discussions on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be time for a break or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This would be a good time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a break, and we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I briefly come back to the small portion of the video that was shown by Ms. Higgins. We have no complete transcript, neither in English, also not in French, and I don't know to what extent it was translated into B/C/S, although the original words spoken were in B/C/S, so that might not cause any problem. Now, the main purpose of the exercise, Ms. Higgins, was that after we played the video as it is in evidence where we have English subtitles, where we have the words spoken in B/C/S, that the main purpose of the exercise was to show that the images shown in the later video, that they were suggestive and unsourced, and that is the only thing. So under those circumstances, the Chamber could exceptionally accept that we do not start a huge exercise in trying to reconstruct everything to have, then, everything on the record, whereas the purpose was mainly to show something, rather than to have full translations, you do not add anything in evidence, so therefore, I suggested that with the consent of the parties that we proceed, and we'll not put an additional burden on those who are transcribing and interpreting for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to point out that we did attach both B/C/S and English translations to the 92 ter motion portions that related to the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if someone wants to look at it, there it is. But, at the same time, under normal circumstances, the transcript of the hearing should be complete, as well, and this is an exceptional circumstance under which we are a bit more liberal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With the leave of the Chamber, I would refer to the portions of the supplemental information sheet that the witness -- that the witness gave, signed yesterday, 11th February, paragraphs 19 and 20 of the supplemental information sheet, which refer to pages 82 and 83 of the Croatian Helsinki Committee report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, do you recall being shown quotes made by General Cermak in the report when this note was being put together?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit this is a clear example of where there's reference to the words spoken by Mr. Cermak, where we see Cermak denied, and you can then see footnote 3 deals with an interview with Mr. Cermak, which in my submission clearly falls within Your Honours' ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever in the report or -- of course, I don't think -- we do not have the -- you're referring to the supplementary -- let me just have a look. One second. Yes, we have the note in evidence but not -- not in evidence but marked for identification. You have not resolved yet which version you're familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have. I informed Ms. Frolich on the break that I objected to paragraphs 19 and 20, which seem to me to fall within Your Honours' ruling because they relate directly to comments made by Mr. Cermak, and I attempted to strike out those portions of the report for the sake of clarity, my suggestion being that paragraph 82 falls away, as does footnote 3. But I seek Your Honours' guidance in relation to that as there was no agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have to look at page 82, whether that's what we see there. Is that this same meeting because it's new to me, the supplemental information sheet; I have not even had time to read it. Page 82 of the report would be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If it assists Your Honour, it refers to a visit by the international commission, the IHF, and it's my understanding that there was only ever one, so I assumed it was the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent that a foundation was to be laid as to who was where and what is the source of knowledge of this witness, that would be the same for what we did before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As I understand, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could please --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- that was covered by this witness, and in fact what Ms. Frolich is now doing is showing him or attempting to show him the statements which were made by Mr. Cermak, which, of course, does fall within Your Honours' ruling because it refers to what Mr. Cermak was alleged to have said at the end of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we first have to establish a basis for that before we continue. You shouldn't ask about a comment unless there's a basis for anything to comment on, and we do not take that from the report, but you have to elicit this viva voce, Ms. Frolich. That's the issue you wanted to raise, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: May I -- sorry, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just seeking a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was just consulting with my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, yes, I asked whether the issue you raised was that what the witness has told us until now about the subject of conversation, that this is not covered by that, and that, therefore, has no foundation for any comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, is it clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I wondered whether you were still discussing with Mr. Kay the matter. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you know -- have you heard of any specific quotes that General Cermak in a meeting that we have discussed before the break that took place with the members of the International Helsinki Federation and the Croatian Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but the witness was asked about what he recalled about that meeting, and he has given evidence about it. We're now coming back to try and do it another way, to come back to the statements which have been up on the screen and called up, as I understand. I object to this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We should take it from the screen at this moment, and in one or two questions you might not have covered everything. You can ask Mr. Puhovski whether he has any further recollection of the discussions and any further details.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, in addition to everything that you have told us so far about this meeting, do you have any additional details about it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I cannot recall any other details, save for the formulation we remembered and that we all referred to when the drills of smoke were being mentioned. The standard response was that people were burning weed. It became such a standard phrase that was also included in the report, and that seems to jog my memory. That is the only specific formulation I am able to recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Puhovski. I will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we seek, Ms. Frolich. Mr. Puhovski, what you just said, did you learn that in that same conversation, at that same moment, or was there -- do you remember that before the break we went in quite some detail through what was reported to you in Zagreb about the conversation that took place in Knin. Now, what you just said, was that part of this reporting during this meeting, or did you learn that in any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That phrase was uttered by Mr. Petar Mrkalj upon his return from Knin, when we talked just prior to the meeting of the seven of us. Later on, he repeated it on several occasions but not during the meeting itself. I spoke with Mr. Mrkalj immediately upon his return from Knin before the meeting when the seven of us met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the others did not -- were not witnessing that conversation. It was just you and Mr. Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was a conversation which was held in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, earlier on in your testimony you mentioned that previous versions of the report had pictures in it, photographs. Why were these pictures not in the new -- in the book version of the report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Because the price of printing such a book would be 25 to 30 percent more, and we did not have such funds.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, could we have 65 ter 7151. Mr. President, for purpose of reference, this is part of a larger 65 ter number that my colleague is calling up. That is the version of the report from 1999, the report Military Operation Storm and Its Aftermath. I selected just a few pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, Professor Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we move on to pages 2 and 3 of this 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, could you just read the dates that are -- the captions that are under the photograph that are being shown, because they are in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: The 28th of February, 1996, for the upper photograph; and the 16th of July, 1996, for the bottom photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And if we could go to next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could you read the caption under the top -- photo on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: It reads: "The police does not set fire in Donji Lapac on the 17th of June, 1998." The lower caption says: "Srb, the 3rd of July, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, I think the English translation of what you said in B/C/S -- it could be understand to mean something different than -- there could be two potential translations of the B/C/S version. Could you explain what the words that are written mean to you, so that we -- they're --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I apologise, they -- as a B/C/S speaker, I would just like to put on the record there are two possible translations of this caption. I would seek clarification from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people you refer to were not quite literate. There should have been a comma after the word "the police." This caption should actually mean that the house involved belonged to the police and that it should not be set on fire. We saw dozens of such photographs with signs: Do not set on fire. The first word of such a phrase, that would be on a house, usually designated the owner of that property, indicating that that piece of property is not Serb property and that it should not be set on fire. This should actually read: The police do not set it on fire. That would be the real meaning, and it appeared on dozens of pieces of property shown on the photographs. Some of those were extracted from our archives and published by the weekly Feral and the daily Novi List.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see such signs on houses?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I did. In the spring of 1996, in the environs of Hrvatska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: For the clarity, where is Hrvatska Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Hrvatska Kostajnica is at the border of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina along the river Una, some 38 kilometres to the south-east of Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Would this be Sector North or Sector South, Professor?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are primarily interested in the photos that are on these three pages, and we would like to tender the photos, not the text because the text is duplicate of the text that is in the report version that we are tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note for the record, I'll leave it to the Chamber, but our standard objection to these, of course, relates to the territory of the Split Military District. So Donji Lapac, for example, wouldn't be within the territory of the Split Military District, so I'm not sure of the relevance, but I'll let the Chamber decide on the geography issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Higgins, any --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No observations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then these two pages, just for the photographs, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three pages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me add one other objection, which is the date would also, absent more foundation, not establish when this was written on these houses, so to the extent that there's a temporal restriction on the indictment, as well, it might be relevant to the Chamber's consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, you told us that you are a -- you speak the language. It looks to me, but please correct me if I'm wrong, I'm just trying to interpret the -- if the text shown below the photograph is the text to the right of what appears to be a door, then I even wonder who can see whether there is a comma or whether there is no comma, but -- so whether the transcript without a comma under the photograph is accurate or not. I don't know, but -- Mr. Puhovski, if you could further ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, the comma was not there. It usually was not used. However, the meaning of the warning was clear: Do not touch. The date was because of the follow-up. We revisited certain locations to establish what was going on. It turned out that the houses which had such inscriptions, indeed, were not touched, whereas the others were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the three pages with photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 7151 shall be given Exhibit P2318. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is admitted into evidence whereas the observations made, of course, will be considered as far as weight is concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Puhovski, in paragraph 12 of your supplemental information sheet, you mentioned that Petar Mrkalj gave an interview to Feral Tribune, which was published on August 28th, 1995, setting out details of crime. I suppose crimes should probably be more accurate. Can you explain what sort of newspaper is Feral Tribune?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: In the period that we are referring to in 1995 in Croatia, basically media space was occupied by the sources and opinions close to the government. There were only two editorial rooms which were known as those opposed to the basic policy of the then Croatian government. It was the Split weekly Feral Tribune and the Rijeka daily Novi List. The Feral Tribune came to be as a satirical attachment to the daily Slobodna Dalmatia, and it was banned as one of the last Communist regime decisions in 1989. The editors of Slobodna Dalmatia, scared by the ban, insisted that the Weekly become independent. It was being published until last year. Partly it was satirical, and partly it dealt with political analysis. It was a rather strange mix. One could see very sharply phrased jokes about the Croatian government as well as about certain other public figures that those from the Feral Tribune did not like, including myself on occasion. The other half of the weekly would be dedicated to interviews and analyses. In the years of 1994, 1995, 1996, it was the only medium where one could come across such views with the exception of the other paper, which was the daily, Novi List.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 7148 on screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, I'm a bit confused. You earlier said that there were only two newspapers, the Feral Tribune and the Rijeka weekly Novi List, that were, if I understand you well, not close to the government, and later on you referred to the daily Novi List. Were you referring to the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think on both occasions I said that Novi List is a daily. It's been a daily since 1903. Perhaps I may have misspoken. In any case, Novi List is a daily and has always been. Feral Tribune, between 1990 and 2008, was always a weekly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to make sure that I didn't miss anything. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, this is an article in front of you, and the title is: It is burning, it is burning; translated as: Dear doctor. Should be: My doctor, I believe. Is this the article that you mention in your statement that was given by -- this was interview with Petar Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: This is the interview. At the time in August 1995, we agreed that we would try to the extent possible to make statements for the public. Colleague Pilso [phoen] published an article in Novi List. Ivan Zvonimir Cicak and Ivo Banac published an analysis in Feral Tribune a week earlier. Next, this interview with Mr. Petar Mrkalj was published. He was the executive director of the Croatian Helsinki Committee. A week later, my paper for the London War Report was published concerning the events in the so-called Krajina. This was an attempt on our part of the Croatian Helsinki Committee to use the three papers that we at our disposal to inform the public reading these papers about the information that we had come by.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the way this interview took place and what was said during this interview that led to this article?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Mrkalj had a long conversation with the journalist for Feral, Vjeran Grkovic, and I personally witnessed a telephone conversation where Petar Mrkalj had to fight word for word the interview being shortened because he wanted the interview to be published as extensively as possible. Mr. Grkovic on his part, the journalist, kept saying that it was impossible for him to include everything that Mr. Mrkalj had said. It was a half-hour conversation where what was discussed what should be left out and what should be included in the interview. This conversation preceded the printing of the interview where that's to say the published version finally carried only a third of what Mr. Mrkalj had stated in the original interview. This is according to what Mr. Mrkalj told me himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you know what was discussed specifically during this interview?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: It had to do with what Mr. Mrkalj came to know during his visit to Knin with the mission in the aftermath of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the admission of this document into evidence on the following bases. Firstly, the interviewee, Petar Mrkalj, is deceased. Secondly, the reporter himself is not going to be called in these proceedings, and there is no ability to test the accuracy of this media report. This witness has only been able to speak to it in terms of being familiar with a conversation he heard about keeping its length, and what he said about it can be gleaned from a mere reading of the document. Furthermore, it contains content relating to the acts and conduct allegedly of Mr. Cermak at page 3 of this media article. It's for those reasons that I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was too quick, Mr. Misetic. I should have given you an opportunity to -- first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just would ask from the perspective of the Gotovina Defence if the exhibit could be MFI'd until after cross-examination, and then I would be willing to put forward further argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: There are no objections to the document being MFI'd at this moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will ask for a number to be assigned and will defer its decision on admission. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P2319, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have 65 ter 7150.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And, Professor Puhovski, you mention in paragraph 12 of your supplemental information sheet that you published an account of crimes during Storm in British publication War Report.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: That's correct. It was subsequently translated and carried in Feral Tribune.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: The document that is being shown to you on the screen, is this the -- the report that you published -- the essay that you published in the War Report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll to the bottom of this first page, and if maybe it can be enlarged in the original. It says: War Report, May 1995. Could you explain this date, Professor Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: This was a typo, just as the 1008 was, because at pages 2 and 3, one can see that it was the August issue. Of course, nobody could know what would happen back in May 1995. They must have reprinted the heading or the cover page from the May issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about whether we're talking about July or August? There is no dispute about that, so therefore you could have even agreed on it with the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I wanted to make it perfectly clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P2320. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2320 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, I would like to turn your attention now to the documentary film Storm Over Krajina, which you mentioned in your statements, and ask you who were the authors or the author and producer of this video, documentary film?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: The author was Bozo Knezovic and producer was my brother, Nenad Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you explain the circumstances in which you were asked to participate in the making of this documentary?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Bozo Knezovic, who I had known for many years, back at the time when he worked for the TV, asked the Croatian Helsinki Committee to provide him with some letters or reports we had in relation to the situation in Grubori in 1995. At the meeting of the executive committee, we decided that we could give that in agreement with the persons who were involved in all of that. I remained in touch with Bozo Knezovic thereafter when he was preparing the material for his film, when he was in touch with people who could provide him with the whole story that he needed to make the documentary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you ever see the footage that was to be used for the film before you were interviewed for the film?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: I saw the portion filmed by Bozo Knezovic himself for this occasion, and I didn't see the copy that was taken over from the Croatian TV Yutel [Realtime transcript read in error, "Utal"] and the TV of Republika Srpska because we did not think it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you see the film in its entirety after it was finished?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: May I just make a correction. Yutel was misspelled here. It's spelled with a Y-u-t-e-l. I saw the film when it was finished. I watched it twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And questions posed to you in the interview, when you viewed the entire film did you find that the statements that you made were taken out of context in relation to the footage that was shown in the film?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I would now like to show several segments of 65 ter 7147, which is the documentary film, Storm Over Krajina. If we could watch the first segment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: "Male Voice 1: I call to leave their towns and settlements into uncertainty but, in accordance with the Croatian constitution and laws, to become loyal citizens of the Republic of Croatia. Male Voice 2: Since the morning hours, the Croatian army has been providing Serbian civilians with food, milk, and juices ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we stop. Ms. Frolich, I hear from the French booth that they were not provided with a transcript, and it's almost impossible to interpret from a running script on the screen. The procedure in this courtroom is that one of the French interpreters follows whether what is seen as a transcript is accurate and that the other one interprets from the written text because it is impossible to follow the speed of speech in the spoken text. Have you provided the booth?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: My case manager informs me that we indeed provided the booth with the transcripts in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I switch to the French booth again. The French booth is trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Ms. Frolich tell the interpreters where they should start reading from in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Very well. Transcript page 13, line 9 in English, and page 12, line 17 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Frolich. Perhaps we'd better restart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Male Voice 1: I call on the citizens of Serb nationality not to leave their towns and settlements into uncertainty but, in accordance with the Croatian constitution and laws, to become loyal citizens of the Republic of Croatia. Male Voice 2: Since the morning hours, the Croatian army has been providing Serb civilians with food, milk, and juices. We are here to offer help for almost 1.000 people. We have enormous columns here. The guys have been working from the early morning hours until 7.00 in this heat. We distribute a lot of food here. We are not stingy, no. One can see that they feel sorry and they don't know where to go. Where are you going? We don't know ourselves. What do we know? We know nothing. Male Voice 1: I don't know what to tell you. Zarko Puhovski: What left a bitter taste were the pathetic attempts to create a picture that all after that has happened the Croats behaved better than any other army that we know, that there were no incidents, that everybody behaved decently towards these refugees or Chetniks or female supporters of Chetniks, more decently than they deserved, which of course was not true."

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, can you please first of all clarify the missing word in the first line of the transcript. And you say "lakurofka" [phoen] in the original. Could you explain that what means?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: This is a word that was borrowed from Russian and came into being in the 1920s as a critical description of the social realism in the USSR where attempts were made at embellishing the reality in the media. So they used the term "varnish." They would varnish like a car the whole picture to make it look nicer. It had to do with the campaign, the goal of which was to portray a picture of what was going on in the course of the operation to show that everything was done in the most humane way possible. This was not the whole truth. It was only a part of the truth, and its purpose was to suppress some of what was going on and some of what we, unfortunately, in the Croatian Helsinki Committee came to know. We were practically bombarded by information that was contrary to that presented.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could you provide a bit more details on the basis for your comment. What specific basis did you have for -- can you give us a few examples for saying that things were represented in a better light?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: First of all, the facts about which this report talks, that there was a series of violations of human rights, murder, looting, et cetera. Secondly, the facts that later on emerged in -- abroad and in Croatia which indicated that there were attacks against the column which had also been stoned, et cetera, and that the people who were part of the column were stopped, even physically assaulted, despite the fact that the Croatian military and police forces escorted the column.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: As for things being represented differently, can you give us a few examples as to that part of your answer or, rather, who was misrepresenting things, if that's what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: The Croatian media, specifically the Croatian television, some of whose footage we were able to see here. In the same film but in the sequence several minutes earlier, the statement of a known journalist was quoted, Nenad Ivankovic, who said that the Croatian army had exhibited a humaneness that had previously been unseen, and this is something that was not experienced by any army, including the Croatian army. And, of course, one could not expect the Croatian population to see the Serbs who were leaving in a better light because they had perceived them as enemies in view of what had happened earlier on, and I could not see why this could not be reported on, even marginally, and that was the gist of my observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Frolich, just as a matter of fact, could you tell us, that portion shown about distributing food and the column, who produced that? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was taken over from the Croatian TV coverage that was broadcast in prime time news on a day in August. I don't know which day precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it in the beginning of August, at the end of August? Was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in the days when the column started to leave, probably on the 5th or the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we play the next segment of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness -- just to complete that questioning, the witness might know where that actually was. It might be relevant for your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be. Do you know any further details about what exactly was shown, what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, this was taking place in -- on the road Bosanska Stara Gradiska, on the crossing and the intersection with the road leading to Belgrade. That would be the way one would take to leave Bosnia and to go to Serbia. Bosanska Stara Gradiska is the border crossing between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know definitely that part of the column turned that way, and I believe that's where the footage was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the parties could agree what -- where to find this on the map what the witness just told us. Whether correct or not is another matter, but at least we know how to situate the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think the witness is right, and it's in Sector North, and I would be happy to point it out, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objections there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think most important is that it's situated in Sector North rather than where exactly in Sector North. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we play the next segment, please, which is transcript page 14, line 10, in English and page 13, line 18, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: "Male voice 1: The Serbs finally left, and I wish them a happy journey, and they should never come back if they like it there. They should stay there. Our Croatia is now free. Female Voice: All these ugly words, all the cursing, when you see a small child showing the V sign, I don't know. Somebody over there shouted at us gypsies. Male Voice 1: What would have happened to you if you had stayed in Dugi Do? Female Voice: The same. Zarko Puhovski: The facts showed that these people were right. Hundreds of civilians were killed after the operation or during the operation, but mainly after operation called Storm, and that showed that these people for these different reasons or at least because of wrong assumptions knew very well what might happen. However, as those small auxiliary columns flowed from smaller places or towards smaller places, some people did not know their geography well. They did not now how to get there, where they wanted to go, and that's why in some smaller settlements killings occurred but not in those large main columns."

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, when you say the facts showed that these people were right, who did you mean by "these people"?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: We have several images of people there, who, when asked where they were going, showed a sign of the finger across their throat, meaning that they were afraid of being -- of having their throats cut or hanged. And I said that they were right because they believed the propaganda before certain events actually transpired, and what transpired showed that their assessments of what would have happened to them had they stayed behind were unfortunately quite realistic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, could we first inquire into what the origin of this portion of the video is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, do you know where this segment was taken and who took it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Croatian television. I don't know where it was filmed. I believe this happened a day later, and it was also broadcast in prime time news of the Croatian TV. But this report is much more correct than the first one because it also shows that some of the Croatian soldiers or demobilized Croatian soldiers were mocking the people who were leaving, which was more reflective of the situation as it was. But I can't tell you what the location is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When making your comments, did you rely solely on the footage that was being shown to you, or was there any other basis for those comments?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI
utterances.text: Again, every day and even at night we kept receiving written reports and letters from people reporting on war crimes. It is true that some of these reports were not true, but some unfortunately were. These were the reports that we received in the weeks and months and years that followed concerning the events triggered by Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, I'm looking at the clock. I'm wondering -- I think your original time assessment was one hour and a half, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I am trying -- I was trying to keep it in the limits. However, due to the objections from the Defence side and due to some explanations with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: -- taken a little more time, I would need only ten more minutes to finalise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we can't have them now because we have to conclude for the day. I can imagine that a careful analysis of the time used would cause you to consider not only the Defence responsible for taking more time, as you said, as a matter of fact, but everyone can do this job for himself. You say you need ten more minutes. We'll consider that. Defence, could I hear time estimates. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I estimate three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I also estimate about two sessions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it very much depends on the cross-examination of my colleagues prior to me, but I can estimate two sessions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which brings us far into next Monday. Mr. Puhovski, first of all, I hope you do not take it as offensive that I'm calling you Mr. Puhovski. That is because I refrain from titles, position, et cetera. Everyone who appears here as witness comes with the same mission; that is, to tell us the truth and nothing else. Mr. Puhovski, what about your availability on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have to be here, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's much appreciated. Now, we have another matter, that we have another witness scheduled for Monday as well. We'll further have to see how we organise that and how much time that would take. I don't think that it will take a lot of time. We have competing witness, Mr. Puhovski, one especially returning this Monday, although not for a long period of time. We'll further consider and further discuss this matter, and it's already appreciated that you make yourself available, although perhaps with some reluctance, for Monday. We will adjourn for the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put your earphones. I was just telling that we will adjourn for the day but not until after I have instructed you, Mr. Puhovski, that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, the testimony you have given already or the testimony still to be given tomorrow and on Monday. We will resume tomorrow morning, the 13th of February, 9.00 in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
